results.reason: The response never says that Varga's stock purchase is a Change of Control requiring Crestline's consent under §15.4. It does not flag that Disclosure Schedule 3.5 wrongly treats the Crestline agreement as notice-only. Open Point B even says the Agreement has no change-of-control provision.

Issue 2 says §14.2 together with the §1.1 'Qualified Transferee' definition allows assignment without consent to any Territory distributor of laboratory or diagnostic products. It notes that the definition does not exclude competitors or their affiliated distributors.

Issue 1 says First Amendment §3.1 restates §12.3 so that only §9 breaches are carved out, which removes the §10 and §11 carve-outs. It notes that §17.5 ranks amendments first, so Crestline's §10 breaches and §11.2 indemnity are now capped.
The response quotes the original §12.3 as excluding breaches of Sections 9 and 10 and the indemnification obligations under Section 11.
The response quotes the §12.2 cap as 'the amounts paid or payable to Supplier in the 12 months preceding the claim.'
The response is a memo with separate issues. Each issue gives the document and section, why it matters for Halvorsen, and a recommended fix.

The response does not discuss whether the Varga deal needs Crestline's consent. However, Open Point B states that the Agreement has no provision on an indirect transfer of Crestline through an equity sale. It also never flags any consent requirement for the Varga acquisition and accepts the Disclosure Schedule's treatment. This implicitly treats no consent as needed, so it fails a strict reading.
The response concludes that the carve-outs were removed and that those claims are now capped.
